title: Nelson Riddle and the 12/8 trumpet part on Lisbon Antigua
summary: Riddle was patient with him, and Edison recalls recording Lisbon Antigua as the lone trumpet in 12/8 time.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Nelson Riddle, he was the most patient man I've ever been with. Yes, he took time out to show me how things would go, you know. And I would ask Manny Klein, say, look, you know, "This is not 'One O'Clock Jump' we're playing." This is something that you're going to have to teach me how to play. And they were all just absolutely fantastic.
I used to keep them laughing because I knew that Nelson Riddle made a date on his biggest hit called "Lisbon Antigua,"

Remember that? Okay, it was in -- had one trumpet on the date, you know, and that was me. Because Gozzo was finishing a date, you know, that he had to do. So "Lisbon Antigua" was just for one trumpet and it was in 12/8 time.
Of course, you're getting all funny time sequences, too.
Let me tell you, I was through with the arrangement before they even started.

They -- they're playing double-time but you're playing just the same time, you know, your time is cut in two. Like the rhythm is playing double-time but you're playing just the regular four/four time. And I said, (humming), but I have to play, (humming). Two, three, four. (Humming). I was through with that before they even started. Everybody laughed about it.
But he obviously used you for sort of solos where he wanted a particular chord. But you had to play --
But you had to play all the ensemble part, too?
So that was a very great discipline for you.
